Neonatal Cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus) emerge from their mothers following a gestation period that concludes with the birth of a single pup, which at parturition possesses a disc width of approximately 40 cm [Lb = approximately 40 cm]. This relatively large size at birth, characteristic of many myliobatiform elasmobranchs, reflects an extended period of internal embryonic development during which the yolk-dependent embryo relies entirely on endogenous nutrients supplied by the mother. Field surveys conducted across the Chesapeake Bay and Gulf of Mexico estuaries consistently report that neonates are fully capable of independent foraging and exhibit coordinated swimming behavior within hours of birth. The substantial birth dimensions likely confer a survival advantage by reducing vulnerability to gape-limited predators, a common selective pressure among coastal batoids. Comparative data from related species within the family Rhinopteridae indicate that a disc width at birth of 40 cm [Lb = 40 cm] positions the cownose ray at the upper end of the size spectrum for neonatal myliobatids, a pattern that aligns with its viviparous reproductive mode and relatively prolonged gestation period of nearly a year.

Under controlled aquarium conditions held at a stable water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], the gestation period for Rhinoptera bonasus has been documented to last approximately 365 days [ab = approximately 365 days], a duration that is consistent with the protracted developmental timeline observed in other large-bodied batoids. This lengthy incubation, during which the fertilised ovum progresses through cleavage, blastula, and gastrulating embryo stages before reaching organogenesis, is energetically demanding for the gravid female, who must sustain both her own metabolic requirements and those of the developing embryo. Puberty in the cownose ray is attained when individuals reach a disc width of approximately 65.3 cm [Lp = approximately 65.3 cm], a size threshold that typically corresponds to an age of between four and five years in wild populations. At this point, testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females commence, marking the transition from the immature juvenile or sub-adult stage to a reproductively viable organism capable of participating in seasonal mating aggregations.

The maximum recorded disc width for the cownose ray, representing the ultimate size achieved by the largest sexually mature adults, is 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], a measurement documented from long-term mark-recapture studies in the northwestern Atlantic. Females tend to attain slightly larger ultimate disc widths than males, a pattern of sexual dimorphism common among myliobatiform rays that likely reflects the selective advantage of increased body cavity volume for gestation. Body mass scales isometrically with disc width, and the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the largest individuals reaches approximately 8,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 8,300 grams]. Foraging aggregations of several thousand individuals, often observed during summer months, undertake extensive migrations along the Atlantic coast, and the energetic demands of these movements place a premium on maintaining adequate lipid reserves, which are stored in the liver and can constitute a substantial proportion of total body mass.

Under the same thermal regime of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C] that characterizes their preferred estuarine habitats during the active feeding season, the maximum reproductive rate of the cownose ray is expressed through an annual reproductive strategy. Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and, following a postpartum recovery period, typically produce one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive output of one offspring per breeding individual. This low fecundity, which is among the lowest recorded for any elasmobranch of comparable body size, underscores the species' extreme K-selected life-history strategy. The extended gestation and inter-birth interval mean that population recovery from even moderate levels of fishing mortality is inherently slow, as each female contributes only a handful of pups to the next generation over the course of her reproductive lifespan. Age at first reproduction for females typically occurs shortly after the attainment of puberty, generally around four to five years after birth [tR = around four to five years after birth].

Longevity data from tag-return studies and captive specimens indicate that the maximum lifespan of Rhinoptera bonasus, when maintained under stable thermal conditions near 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], is approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years]. This considerable lifespan, which places the cownose ray among the longer-lived batoids, is consistent with a life-history syndrome characterized by late maturity, low fecundity, and high adult survival. Senescence in older individuals is marked by progressive deterioration of organ function, reduced swimming performance, and a decline in reproductive output, culminating in physiological death. The disc width at birth of 40 cm [Lb = 40 cm] represents more than one-third of the ultimate disc width of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], indicating a remarkably compressed growth trajectory in which neonates are already a substantial proportion of adult size. This pattern, combined with a lifespan of 26 years [am = 26 years], suggests that the species invests heavily in early somatic development at the expense of rapid population turnover at a temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C].
